abstract: Plants under water deficit produce ultrasonic acoustic emissions that can be recorded in air. Species have been compared mainly by peak frequency. We report, to our knowledge, the first airborne recordings of sunflower (Helianthus annuus) and buckwheat (Fagopyrum esculentum), with gas exchange and chlorophyll fluorescence on the same plants. Across 119 recordings of 30 min each, made on two drought and two watered end plants per species, every drought plant emitted more events over the series than the watered plants. Rates rose 107 fold in sunflower and 5.3 fold in buckwheat, coincided with low stomatal conductance, and later fell in single plants. In sunflower, emission was already raised when maximum Photosystem II quantum yield was similar between treatments. At equal loudness, sunflower events carried a median of 24% of their energy at 40-80 kHz, against 2% in buckwheat, in drought and watered plants alike, although both species peaked near 30 kHz. In a proof of concept on four plants per species, this share identified a held-out plant's species in 96% of draws of five events. Airborne ultrasound thus carries species identity in its spectrum and drought in its event rate, two signals a non-contact sensor could combine.
